input.instructions: Create a compact, accurate blueprint for an 8-to-12-minute educational lesson with exactly ten sequential teaching beats. Do not write full narration. Create exactly three measurable learning objectives. For every beat, provide one distinct complete factual claim, a concrete example, a concise editable visual direction, and one or two exact supplied source IDs. End the claim, example, and visual direction with complete punctuation. Every cited source excerpt must directly support the claim; reuse at least two important technical terms from each cited excerpt so support can be checked locally. Do not invent course assignments, policies, measurements, datasets, instruction encodings, or product behavior that is absent from the supplied excerpts. Keep the claim, example, and visual direction compact; a deterministic local expander will produce the full narration. Sequence the beats from foundations through application and end with a practical analysis checklist. Use only the supplied source excerpts for factual claims. Every factual claim must cite one or more supplied source IDs. Narration must describe information that is essential to understand visuals. Do not imitate a named creator or invent sources.
input.prompt:
Topic: CSCI-529: Seminar in Data Science for Computer Scientists. This catalog entry has student-, instructor-, or term-specific content. Create a rigorous orientation companion that teaches the stable process, standards, planning methods, evaluation criteria, and representative examples without inventing a fixed RIT syllabus. Official catalog description: This course examines current topics in Data Science. This is intended to allow faculty to pilot potential new undergraduate offerings. Specific course details (such as prerequisites, course seminar, format, learning outcomes, assessment methods, and resource needs) will be determined by the faculty member(s) who propose a specific seminar course in this area. Specific course instances will be identified as belonging to the Data Science cluster, the Distributed Systems cluster, the Security cluster, or some combination of these three clusters. Contact Hours: Seminar 3 The previous draft failed local validation. CSCI-529: repeated beat title detected Return only the requested structured lesson blueprint. Produce ten distinct beats with complete claims, examples, and visual directions. Every claim must be directly supported by its cited excerpt and reuse important technical terms from that source. Do not discuss these instructions or include schema examples in any field.

Source excerpts:

[nist-cryptographic-standards]
Cryptographic standards define approved algorithms and parameters. Encryption supports confidentiality when keys and modes are used correctly. Message authentication and digital signatures address integrity and authenticity in different ways. Random number generation supports keys, nonces, and other security parameters. Key management covers generation, distribution, storage, use, rotation, revocation, and destruction. Modes of operation define how a primitive processes data larger than one block. Validation checks implementations against specified requirements. Security depends on the complete protocol and implementation, not only an algorithm name. Analysis also considers side channels and migration requirements.

[nist-ssdf]
The Secure Software Development Framework groups practices into four practice groups. Prepare the Organization establishes people, processes, and technology for secure development. Protect the Software prevents unauthorized access to code and development artifacts. Produce Well-Secured Software addresses security requirements, design, verification, and release. Respond to Vulnerabilities identifies, analyzes, remediates, and learns from discovered weaknesses. Security requirements should be tracked throughout development. Verification provides evidence that selected practices and controls were performed. Security reasoning identifies assets, trust boundaries, threats, controls, evidence, residual risk, and responsibilities.

[rit-csci-529]
This course examines current topics in Data Science. This is intended to allow faculty to pilot potential new undergraduate offerings. Specific course details (such as prerequisites, course seminar, format, learning outcomes, assessment methods, and resource needs) will be determined by the faculty member(s) who propose a specific seminar course in this area. Specific course instances will be identified as belonging to the Data Science cluster, the Distributed Systems cluster, the Security cluster, or some combination of these three clusters. Contact Hours: Seminar 3

beats.claim: The CSCI-529 course catalog designates this offering as a faculty pilot for potential new undergraduate data science programs.
beats.example: A department head might propose a seminar focused on machine learning algorithms to test student interest before full curriculum integration.
beats.title: Beat 1: Foundations of Data Science Seminar Structure
beats.visualDirection: Display a course catalog entry template with fields for prerequisites, format, and learning outcomes.

beats.claim: Specific course instances are categorized into the Data Science cluster, the Distributed Systems cluster, the Security cluster, or combinations thereof.
beats.example: A proposed seminar on secure federated learning would be classified under the Security cluster.
beats.title: Beat 2: Cluster Classification Framework
beats.visualDirection: Show a Venn diagram illustrating the three clusters and their potential intersections.

beats.claim: Prerequisites, seminar format, learning outcomes, assessment methods, and resource needs are explicitly set by the proposing faculty member.
beats.example: An instructor might select a weekly discussion format with peer-reviewed code submissions as the assessment method.
beats.title: Beat 3: Faculty-Determined Parameters
beats.visualDirection: List the five parameters (prerequisites, format, outcomes, assessment, resources) with checkboxes for faculty selection.

beats.claim: The course is structured as a three-contact-hour seminar session.
beats.example: Students attend a single three-hour block per week for the duration of the pilot offering.
beats.title: Beat 4: Contact Hours Specification
beats.visualDirection: Display a calendar icon with a '3 hours' label and a 'Seminar' tag.

beats.claim: The course follows a stable process that allows consistent evaluation of pilot data science offerings.
beats.example: The stable process ensures that each pilot semester uses the same catalog framework and cluster classification rules.
beats.title: Beat 5: Stable Process Definition
beats.visualDirection: Illustrate a linear flowchart: Catalog Proposal -> Faculty Approval -> Cluster Assignment -> Semester Execution.

beats.claim: The pilot course must align with institutional standards for undergraduate data science education.
beats.example: The course description must explicitly state how it meets the department's data science learning outcomes.
beats.title: Beat 6: Standards Alignment
beats.visualDirection: Show a checklist with institutional standards items like 'curriculum alignment' and 'learning outcome mapping'.

beats.claim: Faculty use structured planning methods to design pilot data science seminars.
beats.example: An instructor might draft a syllabus using a template that includes module breakdowns and weekly discussion prompts.
beats.title: Beat 7: Planning Methods Overview
beats.visualDirection: Display a syllabus template with sections for course description, weekly schedule, and evaluation criteria.

beats.claim: Assessment methods are defined by the faculty to evaluate student performance and course effectiveness.
beats.example: Evaluation criteria might include code quality, research proposal depth, and peer feedback scores.
beats.title: Beat 8: Evaluation Criteria Framework
beats.visualDirection: Present a rubric table with columns for criteria, weight, and performance levels.

beats.claim: The course includes representative examples of data science topics across the designated clusters.
beats.example: A representative example might be a seminar on anomaly detection in network traffic for the Security cluster.
beats.title: Beat 9: Representative Examples
beats.visualDirection: Show three example cards labeled 'Data Science', 'Distributed Systems', and 'Security' with brief topic descriptions.

beats.claim: Students complete a practical analysis checklist to verify course alignment and learning objective achievement.
beats.example: The checklist verifies that the course description matches the selected cluster, lists the three-contact-hour format, and confirms faculty-determined assessment methods.
beats.title: Beat 10: Practical Analysis Checklist
beats.visualDirection: Display a printable checklist with checkboxes for cluster alignment, format verification, and assessment confirmation.
